item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.5.0: Full ONVIF and Hardware Transcoding
item.description:
ONVIF cameras could be discovered and their stream URL retrieved — but that was just a corner of ONVIF: PTZ control, picture adjustment, and event subscription, the parts you actually use daily, were missing. And plenty of cameras output H.265 only, which browsers can’t play directly.

PTZ and picture, adjustable

  • Drive the camera with a joystick in the web UI — pan, zoom, one-tap home
  • Presets can be created, invoked, and deleted; frequent viewpoints are one tap away
  • Brightness, contrast, saturation, and sharpness adjust live on sliders, effective immediately
  • Events the camera reports (motion detection, alarms) show up in the web UI in real time

H.265 cameras play in the browser

  • Encoding is detected automatically; H.265 is transcoded to browser-playable H.264 on hardware when needed
  • Freeze-frame anti-flicker keeps the picture smooth through the transition
  • A new transcoding monitor page shows task status and performance at a glance

Steadier

  • The Xiaomi-camera disconnect churn is fixed: a full buffer drops the oldest frame instead of tearing down the whole session
  • Reconnects moved to tiered backoff with jitter — several cameras dropping at once no longer avalanche
  • A batch of fixes: first-boot Docker crash, false health alarms, a login-redirect loop

A protocol isn’t supported until all of it is.

item.title: The Two Devils of PTZ Cameras: Long-Focus Amplification and Dead Time
item.description:
If you’ve used a security PTZ dome long enough, you’ve probably seen these symptoms:

  • Rock-steady at wide angle, but a persistent jitter once you zoom into telephoto.
  • Preset recall is spot-on at wide angle, but off by half a screen at telephoto.
  • Joystick control always feels “half a beat behind” — you push, wait for the frame to change, but by the time it does, the gimbal has already overshot. So you correct, overshoot again, oscillate.
  • AI auto-tracking works fine at wide angle, but the target starts swinging left-right once you zoom in.

Same camera — why is it fine at wide angle and broken at telephoto? Why is joystick control never precise?

item.title: PTZ Stability Four-Layer Defense: From Mechanics to Maintenance
item.description: The most frustrating problem in security projects goes like this: a 36x PTZ camera mounted on a 6-meter pole, rock solid at the wide end, starts to show fine jitter the moment you push to the telephoto end—like someone gently tapping the viewfinder every few seconds. The project team replaces the pole with a thicker one—it works for a few days then comes back. They add an independent stabilization module—useless. Finally they blame the camera head, the manufacturer comes on-site, tests everything, and says all specs are normal. Both sides deadlock, the problem hanging in the middle.

item.title: PTZ Latency End-to-End: From Encoding to Transport Optimization
item.description:
The operator calls: the PTZ feed is several seconds behind. Push the joystick and the far end reacts long after. Ops swaps the camera first—no change; suspects the network—RTT measured, normal; finally shrinks the player buffer—the problem disappears on the spot.

That is not a skit; it is the standard path of a “latency complaint”: swap hardware first, check the network second, and only then get to the real problem. The previous post in this series, “The Two Devils of PTZ Cameras,” named latency one of the two devils. This one tears it apart: where each millisecond goes, what can be optimized, and what is a hard protocol limitation.

item.title: PTZ AI Tracking & Calibration: Gain Scheduling, Dead Time Compensation and Master-Detail
item.description: The site called. AI tracking worked fine at the wide end — the target stayed centered and the gimbal followed it smoothly. Pull to telephoto and the gimbal starts swinging left and right, the swing growing until it finally throws the target out of frame. The first instinct is to turn down the PID’s P — but then the wide end stops keeping up and the target drifts out of frame. Same closed loop, two parameter sets, and neither works.

item.title: PTZ Industry Problem Map & Edge AI Computing
item.description: The security department at our campus swapped out three batches of PTZ cameras last year. The maintenance team’s fault list kept cycling through the same few items: faces in the lobby look like silhouettes under strong backlit daylight, night shots are wall-to-wall noise at low light, IR illumination attracts swarms of insects, and we get dropouts during cold snaps. Any one of these looks like “this camera is bad,” but what’s actually happening is that the PTZ product category is hitting boundaries in three layers: optical imaging, engineering deployment, and collaborative intelligence.

item.title: PTZR Roll Axis: The Fourth Degree of Freedom & Horizon Lock
item.description:
PTZ’s three axes (Pan/Tilt/Zoom) solve “where to look, how close”: Pan rotates azimuth around the vertical axis, Tilt rotates pitch around the horizontal axis, Zoom determines focal length and field of view. Roll (rotation around the optical axis itself) doesn’t decide where to look, only whether the image is rotated—meaning whether the horizon is level.

When mounted on a tilted or moving platform (vehicle, ship, drone, jib, robot arm), a two-axis gimbal structurally cannot keep the horizon level. This isn’t an installation error—it’s a missing degree of freedom: Roll rotation around the optical axis cannot be mathematically generated by Pan/Tilt alone. PTZR (Pan-Tilt-Zoom-Roll) adds the fourth degree of freedom, turning “horizon lock” from impossible to solvable.
